claim: CD4 T cell activation induces nuclear and cytoplasmic actin polymerization via the Arp2/3 complex to activate cytokine expression and strengthen T cell receptor (TCR) signaling.
source: CD4 T cell activation induces nuclear and cytoplasmic actin polymerization via the Arp2/3 complex to activate cytokine expression and strengthen T cell receptor (TCR) signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Actin polymerization dynamics and filament morphology differ between nucleus and cytoplasm.
source: Actin polymerization dynamics and filament morphology differ between nucleus and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript showing different temporal and morphological characteristics.

claim: In humans, the ARP3, ARPC1, and ARPC5 subunits of the Arp2/3 complex exist as two different isoforms, resulting in complexes with different properties.
source: In humans, the ARP3, ARPC1, and ARPC5 subunits of the Arp2/3 complex exist as two different isoforms, resulting in complexes with different properties.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to previous work (Abella et al., 2016; Balasubramanian et al., 1996; Galloni et al., 2021; Jay et al., 2000; Millard et al., 2003; von Loeffelholz et al., 2020).

claim: ARPC5L is heterogeneously expressed in individual CD4 T cells.
source: While ARPC5L is heterogeneously expressed in individual CD4 T cells, it specifically drives nuclear actin polymerization upon T cell activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by single-cell RNA-seq data showing that ARPC5L is expressed in only 46% of Jurkat cells and 15-66% of primary CD4 T cells depending on activation state.

claim: ARPC5L specifically drives nuclear actin polymerization upon T cell activation.
source: While ARPC5L is heterogeneously expressed in individual CD4 T cells, it specifically drives nuclear actin polymerization upon T cell activation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by knockdown and knockout experiments showing that ARPC5L is required for nuclear actin polymerization but not cytoplasmic actin dynamics.

claim: ARPC5 is evenly expressed in CD4 T cell populations.
source: In contrast, ARPC5 is evenly expressed in CD4 T cell populations and is required for cytoplasmic actin dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by single-cell RNA-seq data showing that ARPC5 is expressed in 78% of Jurkat cells.

claim: ARPC5 is required for cytoplasmic actin dynamics.
source: In contrast, ARPC5 is evenly expressed in CD4 T cell populations and is required for cytoplasmic actin dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by knockdown and knockout experiments showing that ARPC5 is required for cytoplasmic actin ring formation but not nuclear actin polymerization.

claim: Nuclear actin polymerization triggered by DNA replication stress specifically requires ARPC5 but not ARPC5L.
source: Interestingly, nuclear actin polymerization triggered by a different stimulus, DNA replication stress, specifically requires ARPC5 but not ARPC5L.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing that aphidicolin-induced nuclear actin polymerization is impaired in ARPC5 KO cells but not ARPC5L KO cells.

claim: TCR signaling induces nuclear actin polymerization via nuclear calcium-calmodulin signaling and N-WASP.
source: TCR signaling but not DNA replication stress induces nuclear actin polymerization via nuclear calcium-calmodulin signaling and N-WASP.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing that nuclear calmodulin inhibition and N-WASP knockout block TCR-induced but not aphidicolin-induced nuclear actin polymerization.

claim: DNA replication stress does not induce nuclear actin polymerization via nuclear calcium-calmodulin signaling and N-WASP.
source: TCR signaling but not DNA replication stress induces nuclear actin polymerization via nuclear calcium-calmodulin signaling and N-WASP.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments showing that nuclear calmodulin inhibition and N-WASP knockout do not affect aphidicolin-induced nuclear actin polymerization.

claim: T cell activation is primarily governed by engagement of surface exposed T cell antigen receptor (TCR/CD3) complexes with major histocompatibility complex (MHC) II-bound peptides on antigen-presenting cells (APCs) (Dustin, 2008; Grakoui et al., 1999; Sedwick et al., 1999; Tskvitaria-Fuller et al., 2003; Valitutti et al., 1995).
source: In concert with co-stimulatory receptors such as CD28, T cell activation is primarily governed by engagement of surface exposed T cell antigen receptor (TCR/CD3) complexes with major histocompatibility complex (MHC) II-bound peptides on antigen-presenting cells (APCs) (Dustin, 2008; Grakoui et al., 1999; Sedwick et al., 1999; Tskvitaria-Fuller et al., 2003; Valitutti et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: T cell activation triggers proliferation and polarized differentiation of naïve T cells required for their development into effector T cells (Constant et al., 1995; Kaech et al., 2002; Zhu and Paul, 2008).
source: T cell activation triggers proliferation and polarized differentiation of naïve T cells required for their development into effector T cells (Constant et al., 1995; Kaech et al., 2002; Zhu and Paul, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TCR engagement triggers the immediate polymerization of cortical actin at the immune synapse, which regulates downstream signaling by facilitating the formation and proper spatial distribution of signaling competent microclusters as well as by coordinating TCR and integrin signaling (Billadeau et al., 2007; Jankowska et al., 2018; Morimoto et al., 2000; Valitutti et al., 1995; Varma et al., 2006).
source: TCR engagement also triggers the immediate polymerization of cortical actin at the immune synapse, which regulates downstream signaling by facilitating the formation and proper spatial distribution of signaling competent microclusters as well as by coordinating TCR and integrin signaling (Billadeau et al., 2007; Jankowska et al., 2018; Morimoto et al., 2000; Valitutti et al., 1995; Varma et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Nuclear actin polymerization following T cell activation depends on nuclear Ca2+ transients.
source: Nuclear actin polymerization following T cell activation depends on nuclear Ca2+ transients, while cytoplasmic actin polymerization is largely independent from Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experiments showing that nuclear calmodulin inhibition blocks nuclear but not cytoplasmic actin polymerization.

claim: Cytoplasmic actin polymerization is largely independent from Ca2+ signaling.
source: Nuclear actin polymerization following T cell activation depends on nuclear Ca2+ transients, while cytoplasmic actin polymerization is largely independent from Ca2+ signaling.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experiments showing that nuclear calmodulin inhibition does not affect cytoplasmic actin polymerization.

claim: Both nuclear and cytoplasmic actin polymerization require activation of the Arp2/3 complex.
source: However, both nuclear and cytoplasmic actin polymerization require activation of the Arp2/3 complex and only a subset of T cells undergoes nuclear actin polymerization, that is, approximately 25% Jurkat T cells and 65% of primary CD4 T cells display nuclear actin polymerization upon stimulation (Figure 1; Tsopoulidis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experiments showing that CK869 (an Arp2/3 inhibitor) blocks both nuclear and cytoplasmic actin polymerization.

claim: Approximately 25% Jurkat T cells display nuclear actin polymerization upon stimulation.
source: However, both nuclear and cytoplasmic actin polymerization require activation of the Arp2/3 complex and only a subset of T cells undergoes nuclear actin polymerization, that is, approximately 25% Jurkat T cells and 65% of primary CD4 T cells display nuclear actin polymerization upon stimulation (Figure 1; Tsopoulidis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data from the current study and a previous publication.

claim: Approximately 65% of primary CD4 T cells display nuclear actin polymerization upon stimulation.
source: However, both nuclear and cytoplasmic actin polymerization require activation of the Arp2/3 complex and only a subset of T cells undergoes nuclear actin polymerization, that is, approximately 25% Jurkat T cells and 65% of primary CD4 T cells display nuclear actin polymerization upon stimulation (Figure 1; Tsopoulidis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data from the current study and a previous publication.

claim: All Arp2/3 complex subunits are expressed in Jurkat CD4 T cells and primary human CD4 T cells.
source: Analyzing the protein expression profile of Arp2/3 subunit isoforms in Jurkat CD4 T cells and primary human CD4 T cells revealed expression of all Arp2/3 complex subunits (Figure 2A)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Primary resting CD4 T cells display low expression levels of all Arp2/3 complex subunits.
source: Primary resting CD4 T cells displayed low expression levels of all Arp2/3 complex subunits, but T cell activation increased their levels significantly.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: T cell activation increases the expression levels of all Arp2/3 complex subunits significantly.
source: Primary resting CD4 T cells displayed low expression levels of all Arp2/3 complex subunits, but T cell activation increased their levels significantly.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The induction of Arp2/3 complex subunit protein levels by T cell activation is paralleled by induction of mRNA expression.
source: This induction of protein levels by T cell activation was paralleled by induction of mRNA expression assessed by qRT-PCR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A: absolute values; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B: relative to GAPDH; note that equal number of cells was loaded and that housekeeping genes are also subject to regulation by T cell activation; Roy et al., 2020; Sousa et al., 2019; Subbannayya et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Baseline mRNA expression of ARPC1A and ARPC5L is consistently lower in bulk Jurkat and primary CD4 T cell cultures compared to other subunit isoforms.
source: We noted that baseline mRNA expression of ARPC1A and ARPC5L was consistently lower in bulk Jurkat and primary CD4 T cell cultures compared to other subunit isoforms and was not strongly increased upon T cell activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: ARPC1A and ARPC5L mRNA expression is not strongly increased upon T cell activation.
source: We noted that baseline mRNA expression of ARPC1A and ARPC5L was consistently lower in bulk Jurkat and primary CD4 T cell cultures compared to other subunit isoforms and was not strongly increased upon T cell activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: ARPC1A is strongly expressed in only 33% of Jurkat cells.
source: Interestingly, ARPC1A and ARPC5L were strongly expressed in only 33 and 46% of Jurkat cells, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ARPC5L is strongly expressed in only 46% of Jurkat cells.
source: Interestingly, ARPC1A and ARPC5L were strongly expressed in only 33 and 46% of Jurkat cells, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ARPC1A and ARPC5L expression is not associated with a particular cell-cycle phase.
source: Since ARPC1A and ARPC5L expression was not associated with a particular cell-cycle phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), we assume that these two proteins are heterogeneously expressed within Jurkat cells, where some cells show robust expression, and the majority exhibits weak or undetectable expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by cell cycle analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: ARPC5L expression levels correlate with the activation status of CD4 T cells, ranging from 15% in resting CD4 T cells to 22% and 31% in memory and activated CD4 T cells to 66% in effector CD4 T cells.
source: Interestingly, the highest heterogeneity of expression was displayed by ARPC5L, and its expression levels correlated with the activation status of CD4 T cells, ranging from 15% in resting CD4 T cells to 22% and 31% in memory and activated CD4 T cells to 66% in effector CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by single-cell RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Selective silencing of ARPC1A, ARPC1B, or ARPC5 does not significantly reduce the frequency of cells that display NFA in response to P/I.
source: Selective silencing of ARPC1A, ARPC1B, or ARPC5 did not significantly reduce the frequency of cells that displayed NFA in response to P/I.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: JNLA cells with reduced ARPC5L levels are significantly impaired in NFA formation upon stimulation with P/I.
source: In contrast, JNLA cells with reduced ARPC5L levels were significantly impaired in NFA formation upon stimulation with P/I but also in response to TCR engagement (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: JNLA cells with reduced ARPC5L levels are significantly impaired in NFA formation in response to TCR engagement.
source: In contrast, JNLA cells with reduced ARPC5L levels were significantly impaired in NFA formation upon stimulation with P/I but also in response to TCR engagement (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B, C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: ARPC1A or ARPC1B silenced cells are both able to support cell spreading and formation of cytoplasmic AR after surface-mediated TCR stimulation.
source: As with NFA, ARPC1A or ARPC1B silenced cells were both able to support cell spreading and formation of cytoplasmic AR after surface-mediated TCR stimulation (Figure 3D and E, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1C for a lower magnification overview and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F for quantification of cell morphologies).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3D, E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: ARPC5 is required for efficient cell spreading and cytoplasmic AR assembly triggered by TCR engagement.
source: Importantly, ARPC5 but not ARPC5L was required for efficient cell spreading and cytoplasmic AR assembly triggered by TCR engagement and cells lacking ARPC5 often displayed aberrant F-actin organization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, and F.

claim: ARPC5L is not required for efficient cell spreading and cytoplasmic AR assembly triggered by TCR engagement.
source: Importantly, ARPC5 but not ARPC5L was required for efficient cell spreading and cytoplasmic AR assembly triggered by TCR engagement and cells lacking ARPC5 often displayed aberrant F-actin organization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, and F.

claim: Cells lacking ARPC5 often display aberrant F-actin organization.
source: Importantly, ARPC5 but not ARPC5L was required for efficient cell spreading and cytoplasmic AR assembly triggered by TCR engagement and cells lacking ARPC5 often displayed aberrant F-actin organization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, E, and F.

claim: ARPC5 KO led to a decrease in ARPC1A levels (to 76%) and an increase in ARPC5L levels (to 240%).
source: ARPC5 KO, on the other hand, led to a decrease in ARPC1A levels (to 76%) and an increase in ARPC5L levels (to 240%) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ARPC5 is selectively required for cytoplasmic actin polymerization and is not substituted by the elevated levels of ARPC5L.
source: Nevertheless, T cell stimulation confirmed that ARPC5 is selectively required for cytoplasmic actin polymerization and is not substituted by the elevated levels of ARPC5L.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data showing that ARPC5 KO cells cannot form actin rings despite elevated ARPC5L levels.

claim: ARPC5L is essential for NFA formation and dispensable for cytoplasmic actin polymerization.
source: In turn, ARPC5L is essential for NFA formation and dispensable for cytoplasmic actin polymerization (Figure 4A and B, see mCherry controls, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-E.

claim: Reintroduction of the respective mCherry-tagged ARPC5 isoform in bulk and clonal KO cells reconstituted their ability to form NFA or ARs, respectively.
source: Reintroduction of the respective mCherry-tagged ARPC5 isoform in these bulk (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C) and clonal (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–E) KO cells reconstituted their ability to form NFA or ARs, respectively, at expression levels that ranged from significantly lower levels than the endogenous protein to significant overexpression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4A, B and Figure 4—figure supplements 1B, C and 2A-E.

claim: mCherry-tagged ARPC5 isoforms associate with Arp2/3 with similar efficacy in CD4 T cells.
source: Similarly, we confirmed mCherry-tagged ARPC5 isoforms to associate with Arp2/3 with similar efficacy in CD4 T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Disruption of cytoplasmic actin polymerization upon KO of ARPC5 significantly reduced the number of signaling microclusters.
source: Disruption of cytoplasmic actin polymerization upon KO of ARPC5 significantly reduced the number of signaling microclusters as well as the amount of tyrosine phosphorylation (pTyr) or phospho-SLP-76 (pSLP-76) within the microclusters (Figure 4C–E and F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4C-H.

claim: Disruption of cytoplasmic actin polymerization upon KO of ARPC5 significantly reduced the amount of tyrosine phosphorylation (pTyr) within the microclusters.
source: Disruption of cytoplasmic actin polymerization upon KO of ARPC5 significantly reduced the number of signaling microclusters as well as the amount of tyrosine phosphorylation (pTyr) or phospho-SLP-76 (pSLP-76) within the microclusters (Figure 4C–E and F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4C-H.

claim: Disruption of cytoplasmic actin polymerization upon KO of ARPC5 significantly reduced the amount of phospho-SLP-76 (pSLP-76) within the microclusters.
source: Disruption of cytoplasmic actin polymerization upon KO of ARPC5 significantly reduced the number of signaling microclusters as well as the amount of tyrosine phosphorylation (pTyr) or phospho-SLP-76 (pSLP-76) within the microclusters (Figure 4C–E and F–H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4C-H.

claim: Loss of ARPC5L has no effect on the amount of TCR signaling-induced microclusters formed or their pSLP-76 content.
source: In contrast, loss of ARPC5L had no effect on the amount of TCR signaling-induced microclusters formed or their pSLP-76 content.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: The pTyr intensity in microclusters is reduced in ARPC5L KO cells relative to control cells, albeit to significantly lower extent than in C5 KO cells.
source: In turn, the pTyr intensity in these microclusters was reduced relative to that in control cells, albeit to significantly lower extent than in C5 KO cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: Inhibition of Arp2/3 activity by CK869 strongly impairs production of TNFα and IL-2.
source: Inhibition of Arp2/3 activity by CK869 strongly impaired production of both cytokines (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: Reducing the expression of either ARPC5 or ARPC5L results in a significant but partial reduction of TNFα and IL-2 production.
source: Reducing the expression of either ARPC5 or ARPC5L resulted in a significant but partial reduction of TNFα and IL-2 production.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: The reduction in IL-2 production is less pronounced for ARPC5L than ARPC5.
source: This reduction was less pronounced for ARPC5L than ARPC5 in the case of IL-2, possibly reflecting the lower silencing efficiency for ARPC5L (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4I, J and Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Both mCherry-tagged ARPC5 and ARPC5L have a diffuse cytoplasmic distribution but are also detected as punctae in the cytoplasm and the nucleus.
source: Both mCherry-tagged ARPC5 and ARPC5L had a diffuse cytoplasmic distribution but were also detected as punctae in the cytoplasm and the nucleus (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Endogenous ARPC5 and ARPC5L are both present in the nucleus, albeit at lower levels than in the cytoplasm.
source: Consistently, immunoblot analysis of nucleo-cytoplasmic fractionations revealed that endogenous ARPC5 and ARPC5L are both present in the nucleus, albeit at lower levels than in the cytoplasm (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The distribution of ARPC5 and ARPC5L is unaffected by the loss of expression of the other ARPC5 isoform.
source: This distribution of ARPC5 and ARPC5L was unaffected by the loss of expression of the other ARPC5 isoform.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by fractionation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Approximately 10% of ARPC5.mCherry and ARPC5L.mCherry spots co-localize with nuclear actin filaments.
source: ARPC5.mCherry and ARPC5L.mCherry were both detected in discrete spots within the nucleus and ~10% of these spots co-localized with nuclear actin filaments; however, no significant difference was observed between both isoforms (9.9% for ARPC5, 13.2% for ARPC5L, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: No significant difference in co-localization with nuclear actin filaments is observed between ARPC5 and ARPC5L (9.9% for ARPC5, 13.2% for ARPC5L).
source: ARPC5.mCherry and ARPC5L.mCherry were both detected in discrete spots within the nucleus and ~10% of these spots co-localized with nuclear actin filaments; however, no significant difference was observed between both isoforms (9.9% for ARPC5, 13.2% for ARPC5L, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: Arp2/3 mediates nuclear actin polymerization in response to DNA replication stress induced by the DNA polymerase inhibitor aphidicolin (APH) (Lamm et al., 2020).
source: In fibroblasts and epithelial cells, Arp2/3 also mediates nuclear actin polymerization in response to DNA replication stress induced by the DNA polymerase inhibitor aphidicolin (APH) (Lamm et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Efficient formation of NFA in JNLA cells in response to APH starts at 15 µM.
source: Consistent with that fact that effective drug concentrations are often elevated in CD4 T cell lines (Martel et al., 1997; Vesela et al., 2017), we observed efficient formation of NFA in JNLA cells in response to APH starting at 15 µM (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: APH-induced NFA formation is paralleled by the induction of DNA replication stress as indicated by phosphorylation of the checkpoint kinase CHK-1.
source: This response was paralleled by the induction of DNA replication stress as indicated by phosphorylation of the checkpoint kinase CHK-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NFA formation in response to APH is transient with a maximum of cells (approx. 25%) displaying NFA approximately 90 min post treatment.
source: NFA formation in response to APH was transient with a maximum of cells (approx. 25%) displaying NFA approximately 90 min post treatment (Figure 6A–C, see Figure 6—figure supplement 1C for tracks of individual cells).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6A-C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The APH-induced NFA meshwork consists of fewer but thicker F-actin bundles that disassemble more slowly than those induced by T cell activation.
source: The APH-induced NFA meshwork consists of fewer but thicker F-actin bundles that disassemble more slowly than those induced by T cell activation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: NFA formation in response to APH is indistinguishable to control cells in ARPC5L KO cells.
source: In contrast, NFA formation in response to APH was indistinguishable to control cells in ARPC5L KO cells but significantly impaired in ARPC5 KO cells (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: NFA formation in response to APH is significantly impaired in ARPC5 KO cells.
source: In contrast, NFA formation in response to APH was indistinguishable to control cells in ARPC5L KO cells but significantly impaired in ARPC5 KO cells (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: NFA formation induced by T cell activation is mediated by nuclear calcium transients and can be inhibited by interfering with nuclear calmodulin by expressing the nuclear calmodulin inhibitor calmodulin binding protein 4 (CAMBP4) (Monaco et al., 2016; Tsopoulidis et al., 2019; Figure 6E and F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
source: NFA formation induced by T cell activation is mediated by nuclear calcium transients and can be inhibited by interfering with nuclear calmodulin by expressing the nuclear calmodulin inhibitor calmodulin binding protein 4 (CAMBP4) (Monaco et al., 2016; Tsopoulidis et al., 2019; Figure 6E and F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6E, F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E, F, as well as citations to previous work.

claim: The nuclear calmodulin inhibitor CAMBP4 does not affect NFA formation or CHK-1 phosphorylation upon APH treatment of JNLA cells.
source: In contrast, the nuclear calmodulin inhibitor CAMBP4 did not affect NFA formation or CHK-1 phosphorylation upon APH treatment of JNLA cells (Figure 6E and F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6E, F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Pharmacological inhibitors of downstream effectors of calmodulin including calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporinA (CsA), calmodulin-kinase kinase inhibitor STO609, as well as the calmodulin-kinase II inhibitors KN93 and KN62 do not prevent NFA induction by APH.
source: Similarly, pharmacological inhibitors of downstream effectors of calmodulin including calcineurin inhibitor cyclosporinA (CsA), calmodulin-kinase kinase inhibitor STO609, as well as the calmodulin-kinase II inhibitors KN93 and KN62 did not prevent NFA induction by APH (Figure 6—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1G.

claim: N-WASP is essential for efficient NFA formation in response to P/I.
source: Functional characterization revealed the specific involvement of these NPFs in distinct actin polymerization events: while N-WASP was essential for efficient NFA formation in response to P/I, WASHC5 was dispensable for NFA formation and loss of WAVE2 did not affect the frequency of NFA formation but was associated with the formation of shorter nuclear actin filaments (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: WASHC5 is dispensable for NFA formation.
source: Functional characterization revealed the specific involvement of these NPFs in distinct actin polymerization events: while N-WASP was essential for efficient NFA formation in response to P/I, WASHC5 was dispensable for NFA formation and loss of WAVE2 did not affect the frequency of NFA formation but was associated with the formation of shorter nuclear actin filaments (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Loss of WAVE2 does not affect the frequency of NFA formation but is associated with the formation of shorter nuclear actin filaments.
source: Functional characterization revealed the specific involvement of these NPFs in distinct actin polymerization events: while N-WASP was essential for efficient NFA formation in response to P/I, WASHC5 was dispensable for NFA formation and loss of WAVE2 did not affect the frequency of NFA formation but was associated with the formation of shorter nuclear actin filaments (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: A role for N-WASP in NFA formation is supported by the inhibition by a pharmacological N-WASP inhibitor.
source: A role for N-WASP in NFA formation was also supported by the inhibition by a pharmacological N-WASP inhibitor (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: N-WASP is dispensable for cell spreading and AR formation induced by TCR signaling.
source: In contrast, N-WASP was dispensable for cell spreading and AR formation induced by TCR signaling while loss of WASHC5 or WAVE2 significantly impaired these processes (Figure 7D and E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7D, E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Loss of WASHC5 or WAVE2 significantly impairs cell spreading and AR formation induced by TCR signaling.
source: In contrast, N-WASP was dispensable for cell spreading and AR formation induced by TCR signaling while loss of WASHC5 or WAVE2 significantly impaired these processes (Figure 7D and E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7D, E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: NFA formation in response to APH is unaffected in N-WASP, WASHC5, or WAVE2 KO cells.
source: Interestingly, NFA formation in response to APH was unaffected in N-WASP, WASHC5, or WAVE2 KO cells (Figure 7F and G) and is hence governed by other upstream regulators.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7F and G.

claim: ARPC5L levels are significantly reduced in N-WASP KO cells, suggesting a co-dependency for stable complex formation.
source: Interestingly, while expression levels of Arp2/3 subunits and isoforms were overall unaltered in NPF KO cells, ARPC5L levels were significantly reduced in N-WASP KO cells, suggesting a co-dependency for stable complex formation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The selective involvement of N-WASP likely reflects that its ability to activate Arp2/3 can be achieved by calcium-calmodulin.
source: The selective involvement of N-WASP likely reflects that its ability to activate Arp2/3 can be achieved by calcium-calmodulin.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: N-Wasp can be activated by direct interaction with calmodulin.
source: This may occur directly via the interaction of N-Wasp with calmodulin, which is known to activate the NPF.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possible mechanism and is supported by general knowledge about N-WASP regulation.

claim: IQGAP can be activated by binding to calmodulin and could induce N-Wasp by direct interaction or via activation of Rho-GTPases upstream of N-Wasp (Le Clainche et al., 2007; Miki et al., 1996; Pelikan-Conchaudron et al., 2011; Rhoads and Friedberg, 1997).
source: Alternatively, the Ras GTPase-activating-like protein IQGAP has been reported to be activated by binding to calmodulin. Activated IQGAP could in turn induce N-Wasp by direct interaction or via activation of Rho-GTPases upstream of N-Wasp (Le Clainche et al., 2007; Miki et al., 1996; Pelikan-Conchaudron et al., 2011; Rhoads and Friedberg, 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an alternative mechanism and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In migrating fibroblasts the identity of the involved ARPC5 isoform affects the positioning of the Arp2/3 effectors Mena/VASP and thereby affects filament polymerization velocity (Faessler et al., 2022).
source: Indeed, a recent study by Fäßler and colleagues reports that in migrating fibroblasts the identity of the involved ARPC5 isoform affects the positioning of the Arp2/3 effectors Mena/VASP and thereby affects filament polymerization velocity (Faessler et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by a citation to a recent publication.

claim: Thin/dynamic filaments may mediate transcriptional regulation following TCR engagement while thicker and more stable filaments could exert mechanical functions during DNA repair.
source: In this scenario, thin/dynamic filaments may mediate transcriptional regulation following TCR engagement while thicker and more stable filaments could exert mechanical functions during DNA repair.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculative interpretation of the observed differences in filament morphology.

claim: The frequency of cells that express ARPC5L is similar to that of cells displaying nuclear actin polymerization in response to T cell activation.
source: Of all subunits, ARPC5L displays the highest heterogenic expression within a given T cell population and the frequency of cells that express ARPC5L is similar to that of cells displaying nuclear actin polymerization in response to T cell activation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by comparison of single-cell RNA-seq data (46% of Jurkat cells express ARPC5L) with the frequency of NFA formation (approximately 25% of Jurkat cells).

claim: The frequency of cells that respond to T cell activation with cytokine production is significantly lower than that of cells displaying NFA formation.
source: However, the frequency of cells that respond to T cell activation with cytokine production is significantly lower than that of cells displaying NFA formation, suggesting that NFA formation is necessary but not sufficient for cytokine production and might also regulate other T cell effector programs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: NFA formation is necessary but not sufficient for cytokine production.
source: However, the frequency of cells that respond to T cell activation with cytokine production is significantly lower than that of cells displaying NFA formation, suggesting that NFA formation is necessary but not sufficient for cytokine production and might also regulate other T cell effector programs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The subunit isoform composition of Arp2/3 complexes emerges as an important parameter that allows Arp2/3 to mediate distinct actin polymerization events tailored to specific activation signals at selected subcellular sites.
source: The subunit isoform composition of Arp2/3 complexes thus emerges as an important parameter that allows Arp2/3 to mediate distinct actin polymerization events tailored to specific activation signals at selected subcellular sites.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Arp2/3 complexes containing different ARP3 isoforms are differentially regulated (Abella et al., 2016; Galloni et al., 2021).
source: Similarly, Arp2/3 complexes containing different ARP3 isoforms were recently shown to be differentially regulated (Abella et al., 2016; Galloni et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Upon immune synapse formation between JNLA cells with SEE-loaded Raji B cells, actin polymerization is first observed in the nucleus and is followed by actin polymerization at the cell–cell contact site.
source: Upon immune synapse formation between JNLA cells with SEE-loaded Raji B cells (Figure 1A–D, Video 1), actin polymerization is first observed in the nucleus and is followed by actin polymerization at the cell–cell contact site.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1A-D and Video 1.

claim: TCR engagement rapidly induces a nuclear F-actin (NFA) meshwork, followed by cell spreading and actin polymerization into a circumferential F-actin ring (AR) at the cell periphery.
source: TCR engagement rapidly induced a nuclear F-actin (NFA) meshwork, followed by cell spreading and actin polymerization into a circumferential F-actin ring (AR) at the cell periphery (Figure 1F and G, Video 2) followed by subsequent disassembly of actin filaments.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 1F, G and Video 2.

claim: PMA/ionomycin (P/I) only triggers nuclear actin polymerization in the absence of cytoplasmic actin remodeling or cell spreading.
source: To specifically study nuclear actin polymerization, we therefore often induce T cell activation by PMA/ionomycin (P/I), which only triggers nuclear actin polymerization in the absence of cytoplasmic actin remodeling or cell spreading.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by experimental observations.

claim: The formation of nuclear F-actin can be triggered by ionomycin alone, but for optimal nuclear actin polymerization, ionomycin is typically used in combination with PMA (Tsopoulidis et al., 2019; Figure 1H–J).
source: The formation of nuclear F-actin can be triggered by ionomycin alone, but for optimal nuclear actin polymerization, ionomycin is typically used in combination with PMA (Tsopoulidis et al., 2019; Figure 1H–J).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1H-J and a citation to previous work.

claim: The formation of both NFA and AR can be blocked with comparable efficacy by pretreating the cells with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK869, regardless of the stimulus type.
source: Generally, the formation of both NFA and AR can be blocked with comparable efficacy by pretreating the cells with the Arp2/3 inhibitor CK869, regardless of the stimulus type (Figure 1C, D, G and J and Video 3, Video 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1C, D, G, J and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: Within the short time frame of the experiment, CK869 treatment does not cause significant changes in CD3 surface expression.
source: Within the short time frame of the experiment, CK869 treatment does not cause significant changes in CD3 surface expression, excluding receptor downregulation as cause for reduced actin polymerization upon stimulation with anti-CD3 antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: ARPC3, ARPC2, ARPC1B, and ARPC5 are strongly and homogenously expressed throughout the clusters of primary CD4 T cells.
source: While ARPC3, ARPC2, ARPC1B, and ARPC5 were strongly and homogenously expressed throughout the clusters, ARPC1A was very weakly expressed and only barely detectable (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ARPC1A is very weakly expressed and only barely detectable in primary CD4 T cells.
source: While ARPC3, ARPC2, ARPC1B, and ARPC5 were strongly and homogenously expressed throughout the clusters, ARPC1A was very weakly expressed and only barely detectable (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ARPC5 KO leads to a decrease in the expression of ARPC1B by almost twofold compared to the non-targeting control (NTC).
source: The levels of other Arp2/3 subunits were mostly unaffected, but the expression of ARPC1B was reduced by almost twofold compared to the non-targeting control (NTC) in both KO cultures.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ARPC5L KO leads to a decrease in the expression of ARPC1B by almost twofold compared to the non-targeting control (NTC).
source: The levels of other Arp2/3 subunits were mostly unaffected, but the expression of ARPC1B was reduced by almost twofold compared to the non-targeting control (NTC) in both KO cultures.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Optimal cytokine production in response to T cell activation requires both ARPC5 and ARPC5L.
source: Optimal cytokine production in response to T cell activation, however, requires both isoforms, suggesting a cooperative function between ARPC5 and ARPC5L for proper cytokine gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data showing that knockdown of either isoform reduces cytokine production.

claim: There is a cooperative function between ARPC5 and ARPC5L for proper cytokine gene expression.
source: Optimal cytokine production in response to T cell activation, however, requires both isoforms, suggesting a cooperative function between ARPC5 and ARPC5L for proper cytokine gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: TCR proximal signaling in response to CD4 T cell activation is governed by ARPC5-mediated actin polymerization at the plasma membrane that occurs independently from the formation of nuclear actin filaments mediated by ARPC5L.
source: Together, these results revealed that TCR proximal signaling in response to CD4 T cell activation is governed by ARPC5-mediated actin polymerization at the plasma membrane that occurs independently from the formation of nuclear actin filaments mediated by ARPC5L.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: The identity of the ARPC5 isoform involved does not determine the ability of Arp2/3 complexes to associate with actin filaments in the nucleus.
source: The identity of the ARPC5 isoform involved therefore does not determine the ability of Arp2/3 complexes to associate with actin filaments in the nucleus, but the association of both isoforms with nuclear actin filaments might be required to induce robust cytokine gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the STED microscopy data showing similar co-localization frequencies for both isoforms.

claim: The association of both ARPC5 and ARPC5L isoforms with nuclear actin filaments might be required to induce robust cytokine gene expression.
source: The identity of the ARPC5 isoform involved therefore does not determine the ability of Arp2/3 complexes to associate with actin filaments in the nucleus, but the association of both isoforms with nuclear actin filaments might be required to induce robust cytokine gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The specificity of distinct nuclear actin polymerization events for distinct ARPC5 isoforms is determined upstream by nuclear Ca2+ transients.
source: Since the specificity of distinct nuclear actin polymerization events for distinct ARPC5 isoforms is determined upstream by nuclear Ca2+ transients, we assessed whether specific NPFs are involved in this process and focused on class I NPFs with reported roles in the nucleus (Teitell, 2010; Wang et al., 2022; Weston et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental findings showing that calcium-calmodulin is required for ARPC5L-dependent but not ARPC5-dependent nuclear actin polymerization.

claim: NFA formation by TCR signaling is governed by a selective pathway that depends on ARPC5L containing Arp2/3 complexes that are activated by N-WASP and nuclear Ca2+ transients.
source: NFA formation by TCR signaling is thus governed by a selective pathway that depends on ARPC5L containing Arp2/3 complexes that are activated by N-WASP and nuclear Ca2+ transients.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Functional coupling of ARPC5L and N-WASP may involve a regulatory mechanism at the level of protein expression/stability.
source: Functional coupling of ARPC5L and N-WASP may thus involve a regulatory mechanism at the level of protein expression/stability.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the finding that ARPC5L levels are reduced in N-WASP KO cells.

claim: CD4 T cells are an ideal cell type for studying the complex regulation of actin polymerization in different cellular compartments and in response to various stimuli.
source: A main achievement of our study is that we were able to capture nuclear and cytoplasmic actin polymerization triggered by a common stimulus (T cell activation) or nuclear actin polymerization by different stimuli (T cell activation, DNA replication stress) within the same CD4 T cell system. This establishes CD4 T cells as an ideal cell type for studying the complex regulation of actin polymerization in different cellular compartments and in response to various stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental work.

claim: The specificity for a particular ARPC5 isoform is not determined by its subcellular distribution.
source: Given that (i) nuclear actin polymerization events, such as those induced by TCR signaling or APH-mediated induction of DNA replication stress, are mediated by distinct Arp2/3 complexes with preferences for specific ARPC5 subunits and (ii) Arp2/3 complexes containing both isoforms are functional in the nucleus, it appears that the specificity for a particular ARPC5 isoform is not determined by its subcellular distribution.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental findings showing that both isoforms are present in the nucleus but have different functional roles.

claim: The nature of the stimulus is critical for the selective induction of actin polymerization by ARPC5 or ARPC5L containing Arp2/3 complexes.
source: Rather, the nature of the stimulus is critical for the selective induction of actin polymerization by ARPC5 or ARPC5L containing Arp2/3 complexes (see schematic model in Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 8.
